title: Occupancy Taxes & Platform-Verified Registration
section: Part One · Module 3 - STR Regulations & Compliance

slides.title: A platform that collects some taxes still leaves you owing the rest
slides.subtitle: Lesson 3.3. Occupancy Taxes & Platform-Verified Registration
meta: Education only. Not tax or legal advice. Rates vary by address.
slides.notes:
A lot of new hosts believe Airbnb handles the taxes. Sometimes it handles some of them. The rest are yours, and the agency expects them whether or not you knew.

By the end of this lesson you'll be able to build a channel-by-channel tax worksheet for one address. It shows which lodging taxes apply, who collects and pays each one on Airbnb, Vrbo, and direct bookings, and what you still owe. You'll know how to enter and keep up a permit or registration number on a listing, and what can happen when it lapses. And you'll be able to reconcile a quarter of bookings against your tax filings before the agency finds the gap.

We'll use Alder Street again, in a made-up tax jurisdiction. Every rate in the example is an assumption for teaching. This is education, not tax or legal advice.

slides.title: Your permit, your tax accounts, and your income tax are three separate things
rows: Permission to run a short-term rental (STR) at the address, and a number to display (lesson 3.1)
Each tax agency that collects lodging tax
An account number and a filing schedule for that agency
The IRS, on your yearly return
Tax on your profit. Your CPA picks the IRS form: usually Schedule E, sometimes Schedule C if you provide substantial services

box.label: Don't mix them up
box.text: A permit doesn't open a tax account. A tax account doesn't give you a permit. Los Angeles lists Transient Occupancy Tax registration as its own eligibility step.

slides.notes:
Two words you'll hear all lesson. To collect a tax is to charge it to the guest. To remit it is to file the return and send the money to the agency. A platform can collect a tax and still leave the remitting to you.

Now let's separate three things students blur together. Only the first two are registrations you apply for. Income tax just gets mixed in with them.

The operating permit or registration is permission to run a short-term rental at the address. The city issues it, and it comes with a number you show on listings. Lesson 3.1 covered that.

The tax registration is an account with each agency that collects lodging tax from you. It has its own account number and filing schedule. A permit doesn't open a tax account, and a tax account doesn't give you a permit. Los Angeles lists Transient Occupancy Tax registration as a separate step.

Federal income tax is tax on your profit. IRS Publication 527 says rental income normally goes on Schedule E, and may go on Schedule C with substantial services. Your CPA decides. Lesson 9.9 covers it.

slides.title: Taxes stack in layers, and every layer has four rules to check
slides.text: Layers: state, county, city, and special districts. Each can have its own agency, form, and due date. For every layer, check:
rows: Which stays the tax applies to
Texas hotel tax: 29 days or less
Nightly rate, cleaning fee, pet fee, extra-guest fee
Where Airbnb collects, cleaning fees are in the base
Only those the agency's own document lists, with its paperwork
Monthly, quarterly, or annual; a return even when you owe nothing
Texas requires "No Tax Due" reports filed electronically
slides.notes:
Lodging taxes stack. You'll also hear them called occupancy, hotel, or transient occupancy taxes. Transient just means short-stay. One stay can carry a state tax, a county tax, a city transient occupancy tax, and a special district charge like a tourism improvement district. Some districts charge a percentage. Some charge a flat amount per occupied night. Sometimes one agency collects several layers on one return. Sometimes you file with each one separately.

Those are the layers. Now, for every layer, check four rules.

First, which stays are taxable. Texas, for example, defines a short-term rental for hotel tax as 29 days or less. Your city's line may differ.

Second, what's in the base. Nightly rate, cleaning fee, other fees. Airbnb says cleaning fees are included where it collects. On bookings you collect yourself, the city's rules decide.

Third, exemptions. Only apply one if the agency's own document says it applies, and keep the paperwork.

Fourth, filing frequency. Many agencies expect a return every period once you're registered, even at zero. Texas requires No Tax Due reports to be filed electronically. A missed zero return can bring a penalty in some places.

slides.title: Airbnb collects some taxes in some places, and you may still owe the others
items: Airbnb lists the places where it collects and remits some occupancy taxes
It decides which taxes apply from your listing address, so an address error can mean the wrong taxes
It may collect regional taxes but not local ones; hosts remain responsible for the rest
For taxes it doesn't collect: collect them yourself, or use the custom tax tool if you're eligible
Custom taxes are charged to guests and paid to you separately. You still file and pay them.
Taxes are added on top of your price. Your payout is your price minus Airbnb's service fee, whether or not Airbnb collects tax.
slides.notes:
Airbnb collects and remits some occupancy taxes automatically in some places, and it lists those places in its help center. The system works out which taxes apply from the listing address you entered. So if the address is wrong, the taxes can be wrong too.

Here's the part people miss. Airbnb says that even where it collects some taxes, you may still have to collect others. Its own example is collecting regional taxes but not local ones. Hosts in those areas are still responsible for checking and handling everything else. Check the list for your address to see which layers that means.

For the taxes Airbnb doesn't collect, you have two options. Collect them yourself outside the platform. Or, if your listing is eligible, use Airbnb's custom tax tool. Airbnb charges it to the guest and pays it to you separately from your payout. You still own the filing and the payment.

And your payout is the same whether or not Airbnb collects tax: your price minus Airbnb's service fee. The tax is added on top of what the guest pays. It doesn't come out of your share.

slides.title: Vrbo remits where it's liable and gives you three ways to handle the rest
slides.text: Where Vrbo is liable, it collects and remits the tax itself. Elsewhere, the owner or manager is responsible. Vrbo publishes its collection jurisdictions by state.
rows: Vrbo, then sends it to you with your payout
Avalara prepares, files, and pays (no extra cost, per Vrbo)

box.label: Under option 2
box.text: The tax lands in your bank account and still belongs to the agency. Don't spend it.

slides.notes:
Vrbo works on a similar split. Where Vrbo is liable for a lodging tax, it collects and remits that tax itself. The return goes in under the company's own taxpayer account, HomeAway.com, Inc. Where it isn't liable, the owner or manager is responsible. Vrbo publishes, state by state, the jurisdictions where it collects.

For the taxes you owe, Vrbo describes three ways to handle them.

One, you collect, file, and pay them yourself outside the platform.

Two, Vrbo collects them from travelers and sends them to you with your payout. You still file and pay.

Three, Vrbo collects them and Avalara MyLodgeTax, a tax filing service, prepares, files, and pays. Vrbo describes that as available at no extra cost.

Vrbo says it always collects and remits where the law requires it, whichever option you choose. The one to watch is option two. The tax money arrives in your bank account mixed with your payout. It isn't yours. It belongs to the agency, and it has to be there when you file. Don't spend it.

slides.title: On a direct booking you quote, charge, hold, report, and pay every layer
items: Nobody collects for you on a direct booking
Your booking engine or PMS (property management software) needs the right rate and base for each layer
Confirm those tax settings against your worksheet before the first direct booking
Texas, for example, puts state tax on the owner for direct bookings and tells owners to check county and city tax separately

box.label: From Sam's lessons
box.text: When you reach Sam's lessons 9.11 and 9.12, find the screen where tax rates are set and check it line by line against your worksheet.

slides.notes:
Direct bookings are the simplest to explain and the easiest to get wrong. Nobody collects for you. You quote the tax, charge it, hold it, report it, and pay it, for every layer.

A booking engine is the checkout on your own website. A PMS, a property management system, is the software that holds your reservations and pricing. Whichever you use has to carry the correct rate and the correct base for each layer. Before your first direct booking, check those settings against your worksheet.

The Texas Comptroller spells this split out plainly. Owners must collect and remit state hotel tax on rentals through their own website, or through a platform that doesn't collect. And when a collecting platform does handle state tax, the owner should still contact the county and city about local hotel tax.

That's one state's rule. But the pattern is common. Platform collection often covers some layers, not all of them.

Sam's lessons 9.11 and 9.12, later in the course, show the direct-booking and Guesty setup. Guesty is a PMS. When you reach them, find the screen where tax rates are set and check it line by line against your worksheet.

slides.title: The number goes on the listing, and some cities make the platform verify it
items: On Airbnb, add it in the listing's laws and regulations section
"City registration pending" and "Exempt" exist, but use them only where the city allows them for your listing
New York City: a booking service can't collect its fee on an STR booking until it checks the city's verification system
That check confirms the number is valid and the host's legal name and address match

box.label: Keep them identical
box.text: Use the same name and address on the permit, the tax accounts, and the listing, down to the unit number.

slides.notes:
Where a city requires a permit or registration number, the platform usually has a field for it. On Airbnb, you go to the listing, find the laws and regulations section, and add the permit number there.

Some cities let a listing show "City registration pending" while an application is in process. Others allow "Exempt" for categories the city exempts, like a hotel. Only use those statuses when the city's rules allow them for your listing.

In some cities, the platform checks the number against the city's records. New York City is the clearest case. A booking service can't collect its fee on a short-term rental booking until it has checked the city's electronic verification system. That check confirms the number is valid and that the host's legal name and address match.

So keep the name and address identical everywhere, down to the unit number. In a city that verifies, a mismatch can block bookings.

slides.title: Calendar every expiration 60 days out and file the renewal when the window opens

nodes.d: Expiration date with a reminder 60 days out. Use the gap to gather what the renewal asks for.
LA: the window opens 30 days before expiration
Check the number on the listing. Save a dated screenshot.

slides.text: Numbers expire. Airbnb's Los Angeles page says the Home-Sharing Registration is valid for one year and must be renewed annually. The 60-day reminder is my buffer (assumption), not a rule.
slides.notes:
Numbers expire. Airbnb's Los Angeles page says the Home-Sharing Registration is valid for one year and has to be renewed every year. The renewal window opens 30 days before expiration. If the registration lapses, you have to apply again and enter the new number on the listing. Failing to renew may affect your ability to host.

What happens when a number fails verification or expires depends on the city and the platform's arrangement with it. In a city like New York, a platform may not be able to take a booking at all without a verified number. So treat a lapse as lost revenue plus a compliance problem.

Here's the routine I suggest. Put every expiration date on your calendar with a reminder 60 days out. That 60 days is my suggested buffer, not a rule. Use the gap to gather what the renewal asks for. File the renewal as soon as the window opens. Then check the number on the listing and save a dated screenshot after every renewal.

box.label: If you miss it
box.text: LA: you apply again and enter a new number on the listing. Your ability to host may be affected. The three steps above prevent this.

slides.title: Reconcile tax owed against tax collected every period, before you file
slides.text: You need three records: the PMS reservation report, each platform's earnings report, and your tax worksheet. Taxable receipts = what guests paid for nights plus taxable fees.
items: Start from the reservation report. Remove fully refunded cancellations; adjust partial refunds.
Split taxable receipts by channel.
For each layer, separate platform-remitted receipts from the ones you owe on.
Compute the tax you must file and pay yourself, by layer.
Add up tax actually collected by layer: platform tax payouts, Vrbo pass-throughs, direct charges.
Compare owed with collected, and explain every difference.
slides.notes:
Reconciliation means proving that the tax you filed matches the stays you hosted. Do it every filing period, before you file. Taxable receipts are what guests paid for nights plus any fees the tax applies to, like cleaning.

It catches four common errors. A direct booking charged the wrong rate. A tax layer left off. A cancellation left in taxable receipts. Or platform-remitted receipts reported as if you collected them.

You need three records. The reservation report from your PMS, with every stay, channel, nights, check-in date, revenue, cleaning fee, and status. Each platform's earnings report. And your tax worksheet.

Then six steps. Start from the reservations and remove full refunds. Split receipts by channel. Separate what the platforms remitted from what you owe on. Compute the tax you must file and pay yourself, by layer. Add up what you actually collected. Compare, and explain every difference.

A shortfall usually means you forgot to charge something, and you owe it anyway, out of your own pocket. An overage usually means you charged tax that didn't apply. Ask the agency how to handle it. And check each agency's form instructions.

slides.title: In made-up Alder City, the operator owes city and district tax on every channel
slides.caption: Cells show who files and pays. "Custom tax tool" and "pass-through" mean the platform charges the guest and sends the tax to you; you still file and pay. Every rate and rule here is a teaching assumption. All layers apply to stays of 29 nights or fewer.
slides.notes:
Now the worked example. Alder Street's standard numbers leave occupancy taxes out of revenue and expenses, because guests pay them and they pass through. In these tables, operator means you, the host. This worksheet shows what that pass-through actually looks like.

I want to be very clear here. Every rate, rule, and collection arrangement on this slide is made up. It's a hypothetical jurisdiction I'm calling Alder City. These are not any real city's rates. Before you use a worksheet like this, replace every row with the official agency's rate, its link, and the date you checked it.

In Alder City there are four layers. State tax at 6%, county at 2%, city transient occupancy tax at 5%, all on nightly plus cleaning. And a tourism district charge of $2 per occupied night.

Now look at the right side. Airbnb remits state and county. Vrbo remits only state. Direct, the operator handles everything. City and district fall to the operator on every channel, even on Airbnb. Custom tax tool and pass-through mean the platform charges the guest and sends you the tax. You still file and pay it.

slides.title: Split by channel, Alder Street's 85 stays produce $61,625 of taxable receipts
slides.text: Channel mix (assumption): 64 stays on Airbnb, 13 on Vrbo, 8 direct. Taxable receipts = nightly rate + cleaning fee.
slides.caption: The total matches Alder Street's yearly booking revenue used throughout the course.
slides.notes:
The first table is taxable receipts by channel: the nightly rate plus the cleaning fee. Alder Street's standard year has 85 stays of three nights, 255 nights, at $205 a night plus a $110 cleaning fee.

I've split those stays across channels as an assumption. Sixty-four on Airbnb, 13 on Vrbo, 8 direct. The course's standard profit model charges Airbnb's 15.5% service fee on all revenue. Vrbo and direct fees are different, but we're not re-running the profit model here. This split only drives the tax worksheet.

Airbnb: 192 nights is $39,360, plus $7,040 of cleaning, for $46,400. Vrbo: 39 nights is $7,995, plus $1,430, for $9,425. Direct: 24 nights is $4,920, plus $880, for $5,800.

The total is $61,625. That matches Alder Street's yearly booking revenue from the rest of the course, which is the check you want. If your channel receipts don't add up to your total bookings, stop and find out why before you calculate any tax.

slides.title: Guests pay about $8,521 of occupancy tax on $61,625 of bookings, roughly 13.8% on top

box.label: One typical stay
box.text: 3 nights x $205 + $110 cleaning = $725. Percentage taxes: 6% + 2% + 5% = 13%, so $94.25. District: 3 nights x $2 = $6. Total $100.25, or 13.8% of the stay.

slides.notes:
The second table is tax by layer and channel, for the year.

On Airbnb's $46,400, state tax at 6% is $2,784, county is $928, city is $2,320, and the district charge on 192 nights is $384. That's $6,416. Vrbo comes to $1,303.25. Direct comes to $802.

Across the year, guests pay about $8,521 in occupancy taxes on $61,625 of bookings. That's roughly 13.8% on top of the price.

For one typical stay, three nights at $205 plus the $110 cleaning fee is $725. The three percentage layers, 6, 2, and 5, add to 13%. Thirteen percent of $725 is $94.25. Add three nights at $2, which is $6. So a guest pays $100.25 of tax on a $725 stay. That's the same 13.8%.

None of this is your revenue. It isn't in the standard profit numbers, and it shouldn't be. But somebody has to send every dollar of it to the right agency. The next slide shows who.

slides.title: The operator remits $4,243.75, half the tax, including all city and district tax

box.label: The trap
box.text: Assume "Airbnb handles taxes" and you'd leave $4,243.75 unfiled, even though Airbnb has 75% of the stays.

slides.notes:
The third table is the one I want you to remember. Who actually sends the money in?

The platforms remit $3,349.50 of state tax and $928 of county tax. That's $4,277.50.

The operator remits $348 of state tax on direct bookings and $304.50 of county tax on Vrbo and direct. The operator also remits all $3,081.25 of city tax and all $510 of district tax. That's $4,243.75.

So in this setup, half the tax flows through the operator's own accounts. And that's even though Airbnb carries 75% of the stays.

A student who assumes Airbnb handles taxes would leave $4,243.75 of tax unfiled each year, including every dollar of city and district tax. The agency doesn't accept "I thought the platform did it." And remember, these are made-up rates. Your real split could be better or worse. The only way to know is to build this table for your address, from the official pages.

slides.title: One quarter's reconciliation finds the operator $12 short on the district fee
slides.side:
The quarter: 24 stays x (3 nights x $205 + $110 cleaning = $725). One direct stay refunded, so 23 stays, 69 nights, $16,675.

Collected = tax guests paid you: Airbnb custom tool (city + district), Vrbo pass-through (county + city + district), direct (state + county + city).

Direct missed the district fee: 2 stays x 3 nights x $2 = $12.

side_box.label: Fix
side_box.text: Pay the $12 from operating cash. Fix the tool setting before the next direct booking.

slides.notes:
Last, the quarterly check. The quarter has 24 stays of three nights, split 17 Airbnb, 4 Vrbo, and 3 direct. Each stay is three nights at $205 plus the $110 cleaning fee, so $725. One direct stay cancelled with a full refund, so its $725 comes out. That leaves 23 stays, 69 nights, and $16,675 of taxable receipts. Airbnb and Vrbo remitted their share of state and county themselves, so those stay off the operator's returns.

Owed means tax you must file and pay yourself. State on direct, $87. County on Vrbo and direct, $87. City on everything, $833.75. District on 69 nights, $138. Total owed, $1,145.75.

Collected means tax money that reached you from guests. $718.25 from Airbnb's custom tax payout, $227 of Vrbo pass-through, and $188.50 charged on direct bookings. Total, $1,133.75.

The gap is $12. The booking tool missed the district fee on the two direct stays. Twelve dollars is small. The same mistake across several units and years isn't.

slides.title: Fill in a quarterly reconciliation by channel and explain every variance
slides.caption: Part D of the worksheet. Parts A to C come first: registrations, layers, and who collects each layer. Every rate needs an official link and a date, or "unresolved". No bookings yet? Practice Part D with the Alder Street quarter from the last slide.
slides.notes:
Here's the exercise. It's a channel-by-channel tax worksheet for one real address, in five parts.

Part A lists your registrations, kept separate. The STR permit, then a tax account for each layer: state, county, city, district. For each, note the agency, the number, when it was issued, and when it renews. Add the filing frequency and the official link with the date you checked it. Income tax treatment goes on the last row, and your CPA decides it.

Part B is the layers: rate, base, taxable stay length, exemptions, and whether a zero return is required. Part C is who collects each layer on Airbnb, Vrbo, and direct.

This slide is Part D, the quarterly reconciliation. By channel: stays, nights, taxable receipts after refunds, tax the platform remitted, tax you owe, tax you collected, and the variance. Then write the explanation. Every variance gets one.

Keep the by-layer detail on a second sheet, one row per layer.

Every rate needs an official link and a date. If you can't find one, write unresolved. No property yet? Use an address you're seriously considering. No bookings yet? Practice Part D with the Alder Street quarter from the last slide.

slides.title: Check the registration number on every listing after every renewal
items: Number entered on every listing, exactly as issued
Name and address match the permit, the tax accounts, and the listing
Expiration date on the calendar with a 60-day reminder
Dated screenshot of the listing saved
Platform verification status checked, if the city verifies

box.label: Part E
box.text: Record the status and the date for each check. Keep it with this property's other paperwork (and the course's SR.1 checklist, if you use it).

slides.notes:
Part E is short, but it's the one that protects your bookings.

First, the number is on every listing, exactly as the city issued it. Every listing, on every channel.

Second, the name and address match across the permit, the tax accounts, and the listing. In a city that verifies, a mismatch can mean the platform can't take a booking.

Third, the expiration date is on your calendar with a reminder 60 days out.

Fourth, you've saved a dated screenshot of the listing showing the number.

Fifth, if the city verifies numbers, you've checked the platform's verification status.

Write the status and the date beside each one. Do it once when you set up, and again after every renewal. It takes a few minutes, and a lapsed number can cost you weeks of bookings. Keep it with this property's other paperwork, and with the course's SR.1 checklist if you use it.

slides.title: Each agency, platform, and adviser confirms a different piece of the tax picture
rows: Each tax agency (state, county, city, district)
Rate, taxable base, stay length, exemptions, filing frequency, zero-return rule
Each platform's help page for your address
Which taxes it collects and remits there. Recheck at every permit renewal.
How the permit number must appear, whether platforms verify it, what happens if it lapses
How taxes and fees appear in your books, Schedule E or C, estimated payments (lesson 9.9)
Direct-booking tax settings match your worksheet before the first reservation (lesson 9.8)
slides.notes:
Here's who confirms each piece. Start with the tax agency: rate, base, stay length, exemptions, filing frequency, and zero returns, in writing or on its official site.

Then each platform's help page for your exact address. Recheck it at every permit renewal, because collection agreements change.

The other three rows are on screen. The city licensing office confirms the permit number. Your CPA covers the books and income tax, in lesson 9.9. Your bookkeeper or PMS vendor checks the direct-booking settings, in lesson 9.8.

slides.title: Four short tasks this week show which taxes will be yours to file
items: List every tax layer for one real address (state, county, city, district) with the official link and date.
Read Airbnb's and Vrbo's help pages for that address and fill in Part C: who collects each layer.
Circle every layer that falls to you on any channel, and find the agency's registration page for each.
If you have a listing, check its registration number, name, and address, and calendar the expiration.
slides.next: Next: 3.4, Red Flags: Markets, Cities & Leases to Avoid in 2026. Bring your worksheet with at least Parts A to C filled in.
slides.notes:
Four things this week, each under an hour.

List every tax layer for one real address: state, county, city, and any district. Beside each, put the official link and the date you checked it.

Read Airbnb's and Vrbo's help pages for that address. Fill in Part C of the worksheet, who collects each layer on each channel.

Circle every layer that falls to you on any channel. For each one, find that agency's registration page. Those are the accounts you'll need to open.

If you already have a listing, check its registration number, name, and address against the permit, and put the expiration date on your calendar.

Next is 3.4, Red Flags: Markets, Cities and Leases to Avoid in 2026. You now have the permission ladder from 3.1, Sam's live search from 3.2, and this tax worksheet. Lesson 3.4 turns them into a fast reject, investigate, or advance screen, so you can drop a bad address in minutes. Bring your worksheet with at least Parts A to C filled in.

slides.notes:
The Alder City rates and the 60-day reminder are assumptions, not sourced rules. These are the main sources behind this lesson, all checked on September 25, 2026. The full list in the lesson has five more. They are Airbnb's pending and exempt page, Airbnb's New York page, Vrbo's tax-by-jurisdiction list, the Texas exemption list, and the Los Angeles home-sharing page.

The Airbnb and Vrbo help pages tell you what each platform says it collects. They change, and they're specific to an address, so read them for your own listing.

The Texas Comptroller pages are a real-world illustration of how one state splits the work between platforms and owners. They are not your rules unless your property is in Texas.

IRS Publication 527 is where the Schedule E and Schedule C point comes from. Your CPA makes that call.

And remember that every rate in the Alder City example was made up for teaching. Your worksheet should cite the real agency for every row.
